class.name: SnowAvalanche3D
class.brief_description: Slab avalanches: release by the stability index, a Voellmy run-out on the snow cover's grid, entrainment and deposits.
class.description: Watches the [SnowCover3D] it belongs to (which adds it while [member SnowCover3D.avalanches_enabled]). The slab is the new snow since it last bonded (a week), or the snow over a buried crust. Where the stability index, the weak layer's shear strength (Jamieson and Johnston 2001, growing as it sinters) over the slab's shear stress (Foehn 1987), drops below 1 on slopes between [member min_slope] and [member max_slope], the slab releases, and the fracture runs through the neighbouring slab while it stays near failure. Loads trigger it sooner (see [member triggers_enabled]): people, sleds and vehicles add the shear under them, and along a buried crust a collapse can run from the flat to the slope above. The released snow runs as a depth-averaged Voellmy flow (Voellmy 1955; Salm 1993; RAMMS, Christen et al. 2010). Gravity pulls it down the snow surface, against dry friction [member mu] and turbulent friction set by [member xi]. Its mass and momentum move cell to cell by second-order finite volumes (MUSCL reconstruction, HLL fluxes), it entrains the new snow it runs over at [member entrainment], and it deposits where it can no longer overcome its own friction. Snow surfaces near the camera break into blocks ([method SnowClumps3D.drop]). The moving snow stays in the cover's cells while it runs, so the snow map, [SnowSurface3D], plants and [WorldSnow] readers all see it move, and no snow is made or lost. Free rigid bodies in its path take its dynamic pressure, 1/2 rho u².

method.name: added_shear
method.description: The shear stress, Pa, that a line load of [param line_load] N/m on the snow surface adds at [param depth] m below it, measured normal to a slope of [param slope] radians. It is the peak over the angle below the load, from Flamant's solution for an elastic half-space (Foehn 1987). On the flat it is 0.207 P / D.

method.name: apply_load
method.description: Puts a line load of [param line_load] N/m on the snow at [param at], [param sink] m sunk in. Returns 1 if a slab released, 2 if a buried crust collapsed (whumpf) without a release, and 0 if nothing gave. Bodies in [member trigger_groups] do this by themselves every physics frame.

method.name: get_collapse_count
method.description: How many times a buried crust has collapsed under a load.

method.name: get_crown_count
method.description: How many crown walls stand (at most 8; new snow buries them).

method.name: get_deposited_volume
method.description: m³ of debris the last avalanche left.

method.name: get_detrained_volume
method.description: The snow, m³, that trees stopped (detrained) from the running avalanche. It lies where the stems took it.

method.name: get_entrained_volume
method.description: m³ of snow the last avalanche picked up on its way.

method.name: get_flow_height_at
method.description: The flowing snow's depth at a point, m (0 when none runs).

method.name: get_flow_velocity_at
method.description: The flow's velocity at a point, m/s.

method.name: get_flow_wetness
method.description: How wet the running (or last) avalanche is, 0 dry to 1 when its slab held all the liquid water it can. Wet flows are denser, slower, rougher and cohesive: see [member wet_mu], [member wet_xi], [member wet_cohesion] and [member wet_density].

method.name: get_flowing_volume
method.description: m³ still moving.

method.name: get_glide_at
method.description: How far, m, the pack at [param position] has glided on its wet base. A glide crack shows from 5 cm; the pack releases full depth at [member glide_release].

method.name: get_glide_count
method.description: How many glide avalanches (full-depth releases of a gliding pack) have run.

method.name: get_glide_crack_count
method.description: How many cells have opened a glide crack.

method.name: get_ice_broken
method.description: How many lake-ice cells the running (or last) avalanche broke through. Ice breaks where the flow's mass over a cell is more than it bears ([method SnowCover3D.ice_breaking_load]); thinner than 2 cm it holds nothing.

method.name: get_max_speed
method.description: The fastest the last avalanche ran, m/s.

method.name: get_max_speed_terminal
method.description: Voellmy's steady speed, sqrt(xi h (sin - mu cos)), m/s, for the flow depth and slope where the flow ran fastest. Compare with [method get_max_speed].

method.name: get_peak_pressure_at
method.description: The highest dynamic pressure, Pa, the dense flow put on [param position] this run ([code]0.5 ρ u²[/code]). Trunks break from about 10-20 kPa, crowns and small trees from a few kPa.

method.name: get_powder_cloud
method.description: The node that draws the powder cloud.

method.name: get_powder_density_at
method.description: The density of snow in the air at [param position], kg/m³: 3 to 10 in a fresh cloud, thinning as it spreads and settles.

method.name: get_powder_reach
method.description: How far from the release the cloud has laid snow, m. It runs past the dense flow.

method.name: get_powder_settled
method.description: The kg of that snow that has settled back onto the cover.

method.name: get_powder_taken
method.description: The kg of snow the last avalanche blew into the air.

method.name: get_pressure_at
method.description: The dynamic pressure, Pa, on [param position] now: the dense flow's where it runs, else the powder cloud's. Systems that break or push things (trees, buildings, bodies) read it.

method.name: get_recent_snow_at
method.description: The new snow since it last bonded at a point, m: the slab that can release.

method.name: get_release_count
method.description: How many avalanches have released.

method.name: get_released_volume
method.description: m³ the last avalanche released.

method.name: get_run_out
method.description: How far the last avalanche's front got from the middle of its release, m.

method.name: get_suspended_mass
method.description: The kg of snow in the air now.

method.name: get_trigger_count
method.description: How many slabs a load has released.

method.name: get_trigger_index_at
method.description: Foehn's skier stability index at [param at] under a line load of [param line_load] N/m, sunk [param sink] m in. It is the weak layer's strength over the slab's own shear plus the load's, taken for the weakest layer. Below 1, the load releases the slab. Use 0 N/m for the natural index. Returns a very large number where there is no slab.

method.name: get_water_entry_mass
method.description: The snow, kg, the running (or last) avalanche put into open water.

method.name: get_wave_count
method.description: How many impulse waves the running (or last) avalanche made: one for each entry into water (an entry ends after three seconds with no snow going in).

method.name: get_wave_height_at
method.description: The height (crest to trough), m, of the run's biggest impulse wave at [param position], from [method impulse_wave_height] at its distance and angle from the entry. 0 when no avalanche has gone into water.

method.name: get_wave_period_at
method.description: The period, s, of the leading impulse wave at [param position] ([method impulse_wave_period]).

method.name: impulse_product
method.description: Heller and Hager's (2010) impulse product parameter [code]P = F S^1/2 M^1/4 cos(6/7 α)^1/2[/code] for a slide of [param mass] kg, [param thickness] m thick and [param width] m wide entering water [param water_depth] m deep at [param speed] m/s down a slope of [param slope] radians: [code]F = V / √(g h)[/code], [code]S = s / h[/code], [code]M = m / (ρw b h²)[/code].

method.name: impulse_wave_height
method.description: The impulse wave's height, m, [param distance] m from where the slide entered and [param angle] radians off its direction: the near-field maximum [code]H_M / h = 5/9 P^4/5[/code] (Heller and Hager 2010), spreading as [code]H / h = 3/2 P^4/5 cos²(2γ / 3) (r / h)^-2/3[/code] (Heller et al. 2009), and never more than 0.8 h (breaking).

method.name: impulse_wave_period
method.description: The leading impulse wave's period, s, at [param distance] m: [code]T √(g / h) = 5.5 M^0.05 (r / h)^0.36[/code] (Heller and Spinneken 2015), [param mass_ratio] being the relative slide mass M.

method.name: is_running
method.description: Returns [code]true[/code] while an avalanche runs.

method.name: stability_index
method.description: Foehn's (1987) stability index of a slab [param slab] m deep at [param slab_density] on [param slope] (radians), over a weak layer of [param weak_density] that has sintered [param age_hours]: below 1 it fails.

method.name: step
method.description: Runs the flow [param delta] seconds now (tests, cut scenes).

method.name: trigger
method.description: Releases whatever slab lies within [param radius] of [param at] on avalanche terrain, stable or not (a skier, a cornice falling, an explosive). Returns [code]true[/code] if one runs.

method.name: weak_layer_strength
method.description: Shear strength of a weak layer, Pa: 14.5 (rho / rho_ice)^1.73 kPa (Jamieson and Johnston 2001), growing by its age over two days as it sinters.

members.member: The mass, kg, of a [CharacterBody3D] in [member trigger_groups] that has no [code]snow_mass[/code] or [code]ground_mass[/code] meta.
How far, m, a collapse of a buried crust's weak layer (a whumpf) runs from the load. Steep slopes it reaches release, even when the load stands on the flat (a remote trigger).

Each release leaves its crown and flanks as a wall of snow along the fracture line (geometry: the cover's cells cannot hold a vertical step), an irregular, rounded line from the bed to the snow surface. New snow buries it.
The snow the flow takes from the new snow it runs over, m per m/s of speed per second, above 5 m/s.

How much snow stems take out of the flow under closed canopy, Pa: [code]K / u[/code] kg/m² each second, so slow flows lose most and stop among the trees (Feistl et al. 2014). Scales with the canopy closure.
The extra dry friction a flow meets under closed canopy, scaled by the closure.

Forest holds and brakes avalanches. Canopy closure from the weather map's canopy anchors the slab: from 0.2 it adds strength, and from 0.5 slabs do not release, by themselves or under a load (Teich et al. 2012). A running flow under canopy meets [member forest_friction] and loses snow to [member forest_detrainment].

Glide: where water reaches the ground under the pack (it drains, holding near all it can) on slopes over 15 degrees outside closed forest, the whole pack slides slowly downhill. A glide crack opens (see [signal glide_crack_opened]) and the pack releases full depth when it has glided [member glide_release] (glide avalanches; Jones 2004; Ancey and Bain 2015).
How fast the pack glides on a fully wet base, m a day, for 1 m of snow on 35 degrees. It grows with the depth (up to 2 m) and the slope, and stops when the base dries or refreezes.
How far, m, the pack glides before it releases full depth, with the neighbours that have glided half as far.
The steepest slope a slab releases on, degrees (steeper sheds as it falls).
The thinnest slab that releases by itself, m.
The gentlest slope a slab releases on, degrees.
Voellmy's dry friction (RAMMS: 0.155 for large avalanches to 0.4 for small ones).
If [code]true[/code], slabs release by themselves when the stability index fails; [method trigger] works either way.

If [code]true[/code], a fast dry front blows snow into the air as a powder cloud. The cloud outruns the dense flow, pushes the bodies it passes with 1/2 rho u², and settles as a thin layer of powder. No snow is made or lost. [SnowPowderCloud3D] draws it.
The e-folding time of the cloud's snow settling out, s.
The share of the front's snow blown into the air for each 10 m it runs, per m/s over [member powder_speed].
The speed, m/s, over which a dry front throws snow up. A wet slide (any liquid water in the slab) makes no cloud.
A fracture opened by a load runs on through slab whose natural stability index is under this value, or under 1.2 times the index where it opened. A uniform slab goes as a whole.

When a dense avalanche stops, the stand where its dynamic pressure passed [member stand_damage_pressure] starts again: 16 m discs of [constant WorldStand.DISTURBANCE_AVALANCHE] go to [WorldStand] in one batch, so avalanche paths stay young (Bebi et al. 2009).
Pa: the dense flow's peak dynamic pressure that breaks mature stems (Bartelt and Stockli 2001: from about 10-20 kPa).

Bodies in these groups load the slab under them: their weight spread along their footprint (a metre at least; an 80 kg skier gives Foehn's 0.78 kN/m), nearer the weak layer by as far as they have sunk in ([method WorldSnow.surface_at]). Rigid bodies use their mass, characters [member character_mass], and the [code]snow_mass[/code] or [code]ground_mass[/code] meta overrides both. Vehicle wheels carry their share of the vehicle.

If [code]true[/code], loads can release slabs: bodies in [member trigger_groups], [method apply_load], and cornices that fail ([signal SnowCover3D.cornice_failed]), which land on the slope below at twice their weight.

Avalanches into water. Over a lake (the cover's water), ice that bears the flow carries it on; open water, or ice it breaks, takes the snow (it melts in), and each entry makes an impulse wave (see [signal avalanche_entered_water], [method get_wave_height_at]).
The yield stress, Pa, of a fully wet flow on its base. It stops thin margins first, which stand as levees, and shortens the run-out (Bartelt et al. 2015).
The density, kg/m³, of a fully wet flow (dry flows run at 300 kg/m³).

Wet snow avalanches. The pack's liquid water weakens its weak layers (see [member wet_weakening]), and a wet slab runs as a wet flow, its friction, density and cohesion following its wetness (see [method get_flow_wetness]). Wet flows make no powder cloud.
Voellmy's dry friction for a fully wet flow (wet snow avalanches 0.3-0.55; Naaim et al. 2013).

The share of the weak layer's strength left when the pack holds all the liquid water it can; the strength is this to the power of the pack's liquid over what it holds (the LWC index, Mitterer et al. 2011).
Voellmy's turbulent friction, m/s², for a fully wet flow.
Voellmy's turbulent friction, m/s² (RAMMS: 1000 to 3000).

signal.name: avalanche_entered_water
signal.description: An avalanche put [param mass] kg of snow into water at [param position], running along [param direction] at [param speed] m/s. It makes an impulse wave [param wave_height] m high near the entry ([method impulse_wave_height]); water systems take it from here.

signal.name: avalanche_released
signal.description: A slab released: the middle of the release and its volume, m³.

signal.name: avalanche_stopped
signal.description: The flow stopped: the middle of its release, the debris volume, m³, and how far it ran, m.

signal.name: avalanche_triggered
signal.description: A load released a slab: where it stood, and the body, or [code]null[/code] for [method apply_load] and cornices.

signal.name: glide_crack_opened
signal.description: A glide crack opened at [param position] (on the snow surface): the pack below it is gliding on a wet base and may release full depth.

signal.name: snow_collapsed
signal.description: A buried crust's weak layer collapsed under a load (a whumpf): where, and the area it ran through, m².
